Why Do We Dare to Trust Tomorrow? The Soil in Which Science Grew
It is the glory of God to conceal a thing, but the glory of kings is to search out a matter. (Proverbs 25:2)

Brothers and sisters, friends, peace to you! When you woke up this morning, what was the first thing you did? Some of you hit the snooze button, some flipped on the light, some picked up your phone to check the weather and decide whether to take an umbrella.

These are such ordinary actions that we never think twice about them. But today I want us to stop and ask a slightly strange question: what makes you so sure the light will come on today just as it did yesterday? What makes you so sure the laws of physics behind that weather forecast still work today?

Imagine if the rules of the world changed every day. On Monday, water boils at a hundred degrees; on Tuesday, it boils at thirty; on Wednesday, gravity is twenty percent off, and your coffee cup floats up to the ceiling. In a world like that, could anyone do research? You probably couldn't even get through breakfast in peace.

Every day scientists measure things in their labs, and quietly, in their hearts, they believe something: the law I measure today will be the same tomorrow; the physics down here also applies to the most distant stars. But that trust is not something experiments prove. It is something you have to believe before you can run a single experiment.

Today we are stepping into the first unit of the History of Science Hall in Creation Speaks, and we are asking a big question: why was science born? Modern science didn't appear out of nowhere. It grew in a particular soil, a soil that believed "the world is orderly and can be understood." Where did that soil come from? Let's look together.
1. Before the Experiment, You Must Believe
Three things you must believe first

Modern science grew rapidly in sixteenth- and seventeenth-century Europe. Many of the people studying nature in that era believed that this world had been made by a wise Creator. That conviction gave science three things it had to believe first.

First, nature is orderly. The world is not a battlefield of moody gods, where the thunder god throws lightning because he's in a bad mood today and the sea god sinks a ship because he loses his temper tomorrow. No. The world runs according to fixed laws.

Second, humans can understand it. People are made in God's image, so the human mind can grasp the patterns of creation. The universe is not a book written in alien script; it is a book we can actually read.
Third, it is worth studying. Creation is good. It is not an illusion, and it is not something lowly. Because it is good, it is worth rolling up our sleeves to observe it and experiment on it.

How important are these three assumptions? Think about a jigsaw puzzle. Why would you spend hours hunched over a table putting together a thousand-piece puzzle? Because you believe the pieces in the box all belong to the same picture.

But what if someone told you, "The pieces in this box were cut at random. They don't make any picture at all"? Would you still try? I think even the most patient grandma would put the lid back on the box and go make a cup of tea.

Science is like a jigsaw puzzle. Scientists are willing to spend their whole lives assembling the great puzzle of the universe because they believe the pieces belong to one picture, made by the hand of one Artist.
Yahweh says: "If my covenant of day and night fails, if I have not appointed the ordinances of heaven and earth," (Jeremiah 33:25)

The prophet Jeremiah uses "the ordinances of heaven and earth" as a picture of how reliable God's covenant is. The turning of day and night, the fixed laws of heaven and earth, are all set in place by God. In other words, the steadiness of the laws of nature is itself a shadow of God's faithfulness.
Friends, when you see the sun rise as usual every morning, that isn't just an astronomical event. It's also a letter delivered right on time every day, and it says: "I am faithful."
Whitehead: a derivative of medieval theology
So how do historians and scholars see all this? Let's meet a few of them.

In 1925, the philosopher Alfred North Whitehead made an observation in his book Science and the Modern World: Europeans' confidence that "science is possible" came from medieval theology's insistence that God is rational. His conclusion was that "faith in the possibility of science... is an unconscious derivative from medieval theology."

That's a fascinating phrase. "Unconscious" means that many people doing science never realized who had laid the floor they were standing on. It's like walking down the street every day: we rarely think about the workers who paved it, but somebody certainly did.
Merton: the Puritans and the Royal Society

In 1938, the sociologist Robert Merton pointed out a close connection between the values of seventeenth-century English Puritans and the way members of the Royal Society threw themselves into experimental science. This idea came to be called the "Merton thesis."
Harrison: how we read the Bible shaped how we read nature
The Australian historian Peter Harrison has done even more detailed research, and he offers two very interesting observations.

First: after the Reformation, people reading the Bible paid more and more attention to its literal and historical meaning. Along with that, they stopped treating the things of nature mainly as allegorical symbols and began treating them as things worth studying directly. Before, seeing a flower, you might first ask what virtue it symbolized; later, seeing a flower, people began asking how it actually grows.

The second observation might make you smile. Many seventeenth-century scholars believed that because of the Fall, human senses and reason had been damaged. So what? So we can't trust our first impressions too much; we need careful, repeated experiments to correct ourselves. You see, admitting our limits actually became a motivation for doing good science.
At this point some of us might get excited and say, "Great! So without Christianity, there would be no science!" Friends, please tap the brakes first.

That strong claim doesn't have enough evidence behind it. The rise of science also involved Greek philosophy, the scholarly heritage of the Islamic world, the printing press, the university system, economic conditions, and many other factors. Scholars accept that the Christian view of creation was one important cultural soil, but how large its influence was is still debated.

Harrison also reminds us that the two modern categories "science" and "religion" were not sharply divided in the seventeenth century the way they are today. If we look back at that time through today's framework, it's easy to oversimplify history.

What we can say with confidence is that many founders of modern science, such as Kepler, Boyle and Newton, openly said that their research was connected to their faith in the Creator. In the next few units we will meet them one by one.

Why do I stress hitting the brakes? Because Christians love the truth, so we don't need to exaggerate. An exaggerated testimony is like a padded résumé: it looks good for a while, and then it's embarrassing when someone checks. The true history is beautiful enough on its own.
3. It Is the Glory of God to Conceal a Thing
Now let's come back to today's key verse: "It is the glory of God to conceal a thing, but the glory of kings is to search out a matter."

When you were little, did you ever play treasure hunt? Mom and Dad hid candy under the sofa or behind the bookshelf, then smiled as the kids searched high and low. The one who hid it was happy, and the one who found it was even happier. If the parents had just put the candy on the table and said, "Here, take it," half the fun would be gone.

God did not write every answer across the sky. He hid mysteries within creation and invited us to explore. This isn't God making life hard for us; it's God inviting us. Exploring is itself an honor. The Bible says that searching out a matter is the glory of kings. Everyone looking for answers in a laboratory is doing something honorable.
God saw everything that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. (Genesis 1:31)

God looked at everything He had made and said it was "very good." If God calls something very good, then it's worth looking at carefully and studying seriously. Studying nature isn't turning away from faith; it's admiring God's handiwork.
Finally, let's consider a deeper question. Why does the universe have order? And why does that order happen to be understandable to the human mind?

Put those two facts together, and they are anything but simple. It's like traveling to a foreign country and finding that the road signs are not only neat and orderly but written in a language you can read. You would reasonably conclude that someone designed them so that you could understand them.

The best explanation for why the universe is orderly and also understandable to the human mind is that it comes from a rational Creator. Please note: this is a philosophical inference, not an experimental conclusion. We don't say "science has proven God," but we can say that all of this reasonably points to the Creator.
Change your mindset and you change your life

Science started with an idea: the world can be understood. One idea changed the direction of human history. In the same way, my mindset determines the direction of my life. Do you believe the world is a random mess, or an orderly work in your heavenly Father's hands? That belief will shape how you face tomorrow.
From man's perspective to God's perspective

Some Christians get nervous whenever science comes up, as if science were the enemy of faith. But from God's perspective, studying nature is not competing with faith; it is looking into the glory God has hidden. When a child finds the candy Dad hid, Dad isn't angry. He's delighted.

When we look at science through the Bible's view of creation, we don't have to fear learning, and we don't have to worship it either. We don't fear it, because all truth comes from God; we don't worship it, because learning is something created, and God alone is the Creator.

Here's a small action for this week: pick one pattern that happens every day, such as the time of sunrise, the shape of the moon, or the growth of a plant on your balcony, and record it for seven days in a row. Each day after you write it down, offer God one sentence of thanks for His faithfulness. After seven days you'll discover that faithfulness isn't just a theological term; it happens outside your window every day.

Brothers and sisters, today when you turn on a light or check the weather forecast, please pause and think: all of this rests on the fact that "the world has laws." And behind those laws is a faithful God.
We can take the order of the world for granted, or we can see a faithful God within it. May we choose the second, and in our studies and our work give the glory to Him.

Lord, Creator of heaven and earth, thank You for giving the world its fixed laws and for giving us minds that can understand them. Thank You for hiding mysteries within creation and inviting us to search them out. Help us to see Your wisdom in our studies and our work; not to fear learning, nor to worship it, but to give all the glory to You. In Jesus' name, Amen.

2. Why is "without Christianity there would be no science" a strong claim without enough evidence? Why do Christians especially need to be honest and not exaggerate when sharing their faith?
3. "It is the glory of God to conceal a thing, but the glory of kings is to search out a matter." In your studies, work or life, what is God inviting you to "search out"?
Eight Arcminutes of Honesty: Kepler Praising God Among the Stars
The heavens declare the glory of God. The expanse shows his handiwork. Day after day they pour out speech, and night after night they display knowledge. (Psalm 19:1–2)

Brothers and sisters, friends, peace to you! Have you ever had this experience: you're balancing your budget at the end of the month, and it's off by ten dollars. Ten dollars isn't much, and a lot of people react with, "Forget it. Round it off and pretend I didn't see it."

Today I want to introduce you to a man who refused to "forget it." Over an error far smaller than ten dollars, he spent years of work and ended up overturning a tradition that had lasted two thousand years.

For two thousand years, people believed the planets must move in perfect circles. Circles are so beautiful: perfect and symmetrical, fitting for heavenly things. The German astronomer Johannes Kepler, born in 1571 and died in 1630, spent years calculating the position of Mars, and found that his calculation and the observations differed by just a tiny bit: only 8 arcminutes.

Eight arcminutes is a very, very small angle, so small that most people wouldn't think it worth fussing over. Anyone else would probably have said, "Close enough. Observational error." But Kepler didn't hide that little discrepancy. He faced it honestly. And as a result, he overturned the thousand-year tradition of "circular orbits": planets travel in ellipses.
The subtitle of today's message is: he meant to become a pastor, but ended up praising God in the orbits of the planets. Let's get to know this honest astronomer together.
1. Eight Arcminutes of Honesty: Kepler's Three Laws
Kepler found three laws of planetary motion altogether. Let's put them in the simplest words.

The first law: planets orbit the sun in ellipses, with the sun at one focus of the ellipse. An ellipse is like a circle that's been gently squashed, a bit like the outline of an egg, except equally round at both ends.
The second law: the line joining a planet to the sun sweeps out equal areas in equal times. So a planet moves faster when it is close to the sun and slower when it is far away.

The third law: the square of a planet's orbital period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis of its orbit. That sounds a bit like math class, but the meaning is simple: the farther a planet is from the sun, the longer it takes to go around once, and it's so regular that you can calculate it precisely with a single formula.

The second law is the most vivid. Have you ever watched figure skating? When a skater spins on the ice and pulls her arms in, she spins incredibly fast; when she stretches her arms out, she slows down.

Planets are like that too. They speed up as they approach the sun and slow down as they move away. They don't speed up and slow down on a whim; they always obey the same rule. The whole solar system is like an ice ballet rehearsed millions of times.

The first two laws were published in 1609 in the New Astronomy, and the third in 1619 in The Harmony of the World. These laws later became an important foundation for Newton's theory of universal gravitation. We'll meet them again next time when we talk about Newton.
Honesty is a virtue in science, and in faith

I especially want you to notice Kepler's honesty. If he had hidden those 8 arcminutes to protect the "perfect circle," the history of science might have taken many more years to get on the right road.

Brothers and sisters, there are many "8 arcminutes" in our lives too. A little something that isn't right, a little unease of conscience, a little place where our lives don't line up with the Bible. Our most common reaction is, "Close enough." But Kepler reminds us that the truth is often hidden in exactly the little bit you want to round away.
2. The Astronomer Who Meant to Be a Pastor
Did you know Kepler didn't originally plan to be an astronomer? He received theological training at the University of Tübingen and was preparing to become a Lutheran pastor.

In 1595 he wrote to his teacher Michael Maestlin with these moving words: "I wanted to become a theologian; for a long time I was restless. Now, however, behold how through my effort God is being celebrated in astronomy."
Did you hear that? "For a long time I was restless." He struggled too: If I don't end up in the pulpit, have I let God down? Later he discovered that God is praised in astronomy just the same.

In 1599 he wrote to Herwart von Hohenburg about the laws of nature: "Those laws are within the grasp of the human mind; God wanted us to recognize them by creating us after his own image so that we could share in his own thoughts."

What a beautiful sentence. To Kepler, studying the universe meant being invited into God's thoughts, to admire His design together with Him. It's like a child sitting beside his father's workbench, watching Dad draw up plans, asking, "Daddy, why do you draw this line this way?"
A saying that gets passed around

Here I need to point something out honestly. There's a widely circulated saying often presented as Kepler's famous line: "I am merely thinking God's thoughts after Him." Many pulpits and many books quote it that way.

But to this day no source for this saying has been found in Kepler's own writings. It should be seen as a later summary, not quoted as his actual words. The closest thing in meaning is the letter to Herwart I just read.
You see, when we're talking about a man who was honest about 8 arcminutes, we have to be honest ourselves. Checking our quotations is itself a way of learning from Kepler.

Kepler remained a devout Lutheran all his life. His astronomy was deeply influenced by his theology; for example, he compared the sun, the sphere of fixed stars and the space in between to the Triune God. Scholars interpret the extent of this influence differently, but it is very clear that his faith and his research were tightly bound together.

Yet his journey of faith wasn't smooth either. From 1612 on, because he could not accept some of the teachings in the Formula of Concord, the pastor in Linz barred him from Holy Communion. A man who loved the Lord all his life, kept away from the Lord's table: how painful that must have been.
The heavens declare the glory of God. The expanse shows his handiwork. (Psalm 19:1)
Kepler's life is a footnote to this verse. The heavens don't speak, yet day and night they proclaim God's handiwork. And Kepler was a man who translated the speech of the heavens into mathematics.
3. Still Looking Up at the Stars in Suffering
A life that was far from easy

By now you might imagine Kepler had a glamorous life. Not at all. His life was hard: his wife and children died young, he was driven from place to place by war, and his own mother was even accused of witchcraft, and he personally defended her.

Think about it. A man who studies the most orderly, most harmonious things in the heavens, while his own life is a complete mess. Wouldn't you want to ask, "God, You've arranged the stars so well, why can't You arrange my life a little better?"
And yet in his suffering, Kepler still looked up to the order of the heavens.

Lift up your eyes on high, and see who has created these, who brings out their army by number. He calls them all by name. By the greatness of his might, and because he is strong in power, not one is lacking. (Isaiah 40:26)

This verse says God brings out the stars by number and calls each one by name, and not one is missing. For thousands upon thousands of years the planets have followed the same laws; what Kepler saw was an orderly and faithful God.
Brothers and sisters, if God won't miss even one star in the sky, will He miss you? Your tears, your troubles, He knows them all.

When I consider your heavens, the work of your fingers, the moon and the stars, which you have ordained; what is man, that you think of him? What is the son of man, that you care for him? (Psalm 8:3–4)

The universe is so vast, and we are so small. But the psalmist says this God who made the heavens actually thinks of us and cares for us. The starry sky isn't meant to make us feel too small to matter; it's meant to amaze us: such a great God actually cares about me.
Elegant mathematics points to a rational Creator

There's one more thing worth pondering. The universe can be described by elegant mathematics, like Kepler's three laws; and the human mind happens to be able to understand that mathematics. Put those two things together, and it's reasonable to conclude that there is a rational Creator behind it. This is a philosophical inference, not an experimental proof, but it is a weighty pointer.

Over an error of 8 arcminutes, Kepler rethought all of astronomy. In the eight steps of changing our mindset, review and correction are the keys to growth. Those who refuse to review keep walking in circles all their lives; only those willing to be corrected can walk the orbit God has for them.
Let Jesus receive all the glory

Kepler wasn't a pastor by profession, yet in astronomy he brought praise to God. You may be an accountant, a teacher, an engineer or a homemaker, and your work too can let Jesus receive all the glory. The pulpit isn't the only altar; your desk, your kitchen and your classroom can all be altars too.
The Holy Spirit is my guide
Keep looking up even in hard times, and ask the Holy Spirit to guide me along God's orbit. The planets don't keep to their orbits by their own strength, and neither do we.

This week's action: identify one opinion you've held onto for a long time that might need correcting. Bring it to God in prayer, and share it honestly with one of your spiritual companions. That's your "8 arcminutes."

Brothers and sisters, tonight, find a moment to look up at the sky. Find a planet or the brightest star, and think about how it is moving along the orbit God has set. It doesn't make a fuss, yet day and night it declares the glory of God.
And ask yourself: when the facts don't match what I originally thought, am I willing to face them honestly like Kepler, or will I keep only the answers I like?

Heavenly Father, the heavens declare Your glory. Thank You for letting us understand the laws You have set, and thank You for caring for us even in our suffering. Make us honest and humble, willing to be corrected by the truth, both in our learning and in our lives. May our work also become a song of praise to You. In Jesus' name, Amen.

2. Kepler said God is praised in astronomy too. How can your work or daily life bring praise to God?

3. Kepler kept looking up while suffering the early deaths of his wife and children, displacement by war and his mother's accusation. When your life seems to have no order, what comfort do Isaiah 40:26 and Psalm 8:3–4 give you?
The First to Plead Seems Right: The Truth About the Galileo Affair
He who pleads his cause first seems right; until another comes and questions him. (Proverbs 18:17)

Brothers and sisters, friends, peace to you! Parents with more than one child will know this scene well: the oldest runs in crying, "My little brother hit me!" Just as you're about to lose your temper, the little brother runs in too: "He grabbed my toy first!" Ask a few more questions, and it turns out the toy was lent to the little brother by their sister, and the oldest thought it was his...

Friends, in nine out of ten of these household "cases," if you only hear one side, you'll get the verdict wrong. King Solomon saw through this long ago: "He who pleads his cause first seems right; until another comes and questions him."

Today we're going to look at one of the most famous "cases" in history: the Galileo affair. Many people have heard this version of the story: because Galileo said the earth goes around the sun, the Church threw him in prison and tortured him, and as he was led away he muttered, "And yet it moves."

That story is very dramatic, perfect for a movie. But the real history is more complicated than that story, and more worth reflecting on. Today's subtitle is: it wasn't as simple as "science versus religion," and the Church wasn't blameless either. We need to hear both sides to find out what really happened.
Let's lay out the timeline first, like a detective organizing a case file.

In 1610, Galileo used his telescope to see the moons of Jupiter and the phases of Venus, observations that supported Copernicus's sun-centered model. Galileo was born in 1564, so by then he was in his forties, at the peak of his research.
In 1616, the Roman Congregation of the Index declared heliocentrism contrary to Scripture, and Galileo was warned not to hold or defend it.

In 1632, he published the Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems. The book has a character called "Simplicio," and Galileo put Pope Urban VIII's arguments into this character's mouth. You can imagine: it's like writing a novel, putting your boss's favorite sayings into the mouth of the character who looks least intelligent, and then publishing it. How would your boss feel when he read it?

In 1633, the Inquisition found him "vehemently suspected of heresy" and required him to publicly renounce heliocentrism. He was sentenced to imprisonment, which was immediately commuted to house arrest. He spent the rest of his life at Arcetri near Florence and died in 1642.
Now let's compare this with the popular story.
First, Galileo really was subjected to an unjust trial, forced to recant and placed under house arrest. That's a fact. But he was not put in prison.

Second, in 2009 the historian of science Ronald Numbers edited Galileo Goes to Jail and Other Myths about Science and Religion. In it, Maurice Finocchiaro points out that during his interrogation Galileo was threatened with torture, but there is no evidence that torture was actually used. "Prison" and "torture" are later exaggerations.

Third, the famous line "And yet it moves" first appears in a 1757 work by Baretti, more than a hundred years after the trial. Neither the trial records of the time nor the biography written by his student mention it, and it is generally regarded as legend.

It's a great line, I admit, but it was very likely written for Galileo by later generations. It's like the many celebrity quotes that circulate online; the celebrity might well read one and say, "Did I ever say that?"
2. The Truth Is More Complicated Than a Slogan
A family quarrel retold as good versus evil

The Galileo affair is like a family quarrel that got retold as a story of "good guys versus bad guys." The truth involves power, saving face and academic factions, as well as genuine scientific questions. If we reduce it to a slogan, we miss the real lessons.

For example, Galileo himself was a Catholic, and he did not oppose the Bible. In 1615, in his Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina, he quoted a saying of Cardinal Baronius: "the intention of the Holy Spirit is to teach us how one goes to heaven and not how heaven goes."

That's beautifully put. The Bible is not an astronomy textbook; its focus is leading people to know God and receive salvation. Galileo didn't set science and faith against each other; he was thinking about how each could keep to its proper role.
The real scientific problems of the time
There's another thing many people don't know: at that time, heliocentrism still faced real scientific problems.

For example, if the earth goes around the sun, you should in theory be able to observe "stellar parallax." But it couldn't be observed then; it wasn't actually measured until 1838. Another example: Galileo used the tides to argue that the earth moves, and that argument later turned out to be wrong.
So those who opposed heliocentrism at the time were not all just stubborn; some had genuine scientific doubts. All of this means the affair wasn't simply black and white, right versus wrong.
A breakdown of power and relationships

Historians also point out that besides theology and science, the Galileo affair involved the breakdown of his relationship with the Pope, as well as academic and political power struggles. How much weight each factor carried is still debated by historians.

Brothers and sisters, have you noticed? Many conflicts look like "disagreements over ideas" on the surface, but underneath they are "struggles over saving face." That isn't just a seventeenth-century thing; it plays out every day in our church small groups and around our family dinner tables.

When a husband and wife argue, are they really arguing about whether to squeeze the toothpaste from the middle or the end? Usually not. They're arguing about "do you care how I feel?" When church volunteers get red in the face in a meeting, are they really arguing about whether the chairs go in a circle or in rows? Usually not either. When we can see the heart beneath the pride, many quarrels can quiet down.
3. Truth Is Not Afraid to Be Examined
Lesson one: don't attack others with simplified stories
This piece of history gives us two lessons. First: don't attack others with simplified stories.

Today some people use the "Galileo was jailed and tortured" version to attack faith; on the other side, some Christians use simplified stories to attack scientists. Both make the same mistake: they listen only to the one who pleads first and don't wait for the other to come and question him.
You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free. (John 8:32)

The Lord Jesus said the truth will make us free. People who love the truth aren't afraid to get to the bottom of things, because the truth doesn't need exaggeration to protect it or concealment to keep it standing.
Lesson two: when the church is wrong, admit it honestly
The second lesson: when the church has done wrong, we should admit it honestly and not make excuses for it.

In 1992, Pope John Paul II, in an address to the Pontifical Academy of Sciences, acknowledged that the theologians of that time had misunderstood Scripture. From 1633 to 1992 is a road of more than three hundred years, but admitting it is still better than never admitting it.
God is righteous. He does not need anyone to protect His name by unrighteous means. When God's people use power to crush others, it is precisely God's name that gets damaged.
If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. (1 John 1:9)

Friends, confessing isn't weakness; confessing is coming back into the light. That's true for individuals, and it's true for the church. A church that dares to say "we were wrong" actually lets people see God's faithfulness and righteousness more clearly.

Scripture and nature both come from the same God. Real conflict exists only in people's mistaken interpretations of the two. This is a theological and philosophical inference, and it's a very important key when we face questions about science and faith.
It's like two books written by the same author: if they seem to contradict each other, it's more likely the reader has misread them than that the author made a mistake.
He has shown you, O man, what is good. What does Yahweh require of you, but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God? (Micah 6:8)
To act justly, to love mercy, to walk humbly. If everyone involved in the affair back then had taken this verse to heart, history might have been written very differently.

There was pride on both sides of the affair. Some were proud of their power, some proud of their brilliance, even putting the other side's arguments into the mouth of a foolish-looking character. Humility overcomes pride: it means returning to our proper place, letting God be God, not crushing people with power, and not humiliating them with cleverness.

When we argue about ideas, we must not hurt people. The person sitting across from you is someone God loves, not an enemy to be defeated. We can debate ideas, but we must never trample people just to win.
Letting Jesus reign means: the point isn't that I win, but that the truth prevails. When I say "let Jesus reign," I step down from the throne of "I have to prove I'm right."

This week's action: the next time you hear a story about how "such-and-such group is terrible," check what the other side says before deciding whether to pass it on. Be the "other who comes and questions," and help everyone find out what really happened.

Brothers and sisters, please be still for a moment and think about times you jumped to a conclusion after hearing only one side. And think about this: when I, or a group I belong to, get something wrong, do I rush to defend it, or am I willing to admit it before God?

The Galileo affair is neither a victory song of science over religion nor a defense of the Church's innocence. It's a mirror that reveals the pride that can live in every human heart. And the good news of the gospel is this: whoever confesses, God is faithful and will forgive.

Righteous God, forgive us for the times we have put pride and power in the place of truth, and forgive us for the times we have judged others after hearing only one side. Make us love the truth and speak honestly, and make Your church humble and teachable. In every argument, may we let Jesus reign. In Jesus' name, Amen.

2. Galileo quoted the saying that "the intention of the Holy Spirit is to teach us how one goes to heaven and not how heaven goes." How do you understand this? How does it help us read the Bible?
3. Have you ever misjudged someone because you heard only one side? How can you put Proverbs 18:17 into practice this week and be someone who "finds out what really happened"?
The Apple and the Moon: The Laws Newton Saw, and the Lord Behind Them
He is before all things, and in him all things are held together. (Colossians 1:17)
Brothers and sisters, friends, peace to you! I'd like to start by asking you to do a little experiment. Pick up something small near you, a pen or a key, and gently let go of it. Let it fall.
Okay, it fell. Nobody's pen floated up, right? If it did, please come and see me after the service. We need to have a serious talk.

It's a simple action that even a three-year-old can do. But one man looked at something this simple and asked a far-from-simple question: an apple falls to the ground, so why doesn't the moon fall down?

That man was Isaac Newton, born in 1643 and died in 1727. His insight was that the force that makes an apple fall and the force that holds the moon are actually one and the same. Today's subtitle is: the same law that governs the falling apple also governs the moon in its course.
Today we'll look at three things: what laws Newton saw; how he viewed the One behind the laws; and how we should honestly deal with Newton's faith.
1. One Law for Heaven and Earth
Heaven and earth united for the first time
Before Newton, many people had a sense that the heavens were the heavens and the earth was the earth, two worlds each with its own rules.

In 1687, Newton published the Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy. Using a single set of mathematics, he explained falling bodies on earth, planets in the sky and the tides in the sea. For the first time, heaven and earth were united under the same set of laws.

It's as if you'd always thought the lights, the fridge and the air conditioner in your home each had its own power supply, and then one day the electrician told you, "Actually, they're all connected to the same main switch." Suddenly it clicks: they're one family!

Newton proposed three laws of motion. First, inertia: if nothing pushes an object, it stays as it is. Second, force equals mass times acceleration. Third, action and reaction: when you push a wall, the wall pushes back on you.

Then comes universal gravitation: any two objects attract each other, and the force is proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.

What does "inversely proportional to the square of the distance" mean? It means that if you double the distance, the pull becomes a quarter of what it was. So the farther away you are, the faster the pull weakens.

That reminds me of our relationship with God. Some people say, "I've only drifted a little away from God. It's no big deal." But spiritual distance often works the same way: the farther you go, the weaker the pull, and it weakens faster than you think. One step away today, and tomorrow church feels optional; the day after, you can't even remember to pray. So draw near to God, and do it early.

The most beautiful part is that Kepler's three laws of planetary motion can be derived from these laws. The rules Kepler, in our last unit, spent years digging out of observational data one by one, Newton explained all at once with a few laws.

So why doesn't the moon fall? The answer is wonderful: the moon is actually "falling" toward the earth all the time, but it's also moving sideways fast enough that it never falls down, so it keeps circling the earth.

It's like swinging a ball on a string: the tension in the string is gravity. Let go, and the ball flies off; hold the string, and the ball circles obediently. In the universe there is an invisible string holding the moon, and holding us too.

As for the story that "Newton thought of gravity when he saw an apple fall," it comes from his own recollections to a friend in his old age. The details may have been embellished later, but it's not a complete fabrication. So next time you tell the story, go ahead, but there's no need to add special effects like "the apple landed right on his head."
2. The Most Beautiful System Comes from a Wise Lord

How did Newton view the meaning behind these laws? In 1713, the second edition of the Principia added an essay called the General Scholium. In it Newton wrote: "This most elegant system of the sun, planets, and comets could not have arisen without the design and dominion of an intelligent and powerful being."
He also said that this Being "rules all things, not as the world soul but as the lord of all."
Please notice this distinction. Newton didn't see God as merely some energy or soul inside the universe, but as the Lord above the universe, governing all things.
Hoping to help people believe in God

Earlier still, in 1692, Newton wrote to Richard Bentley, who was giving the Boyle Lectures. He said that when he wrote the book, he had hoped its principles could help thoughtful people believe in a God.
Friends, this is one of the most important scientific works in human history, and what its author hoped for was that readers would think of God.

The laws of nature are stable, universal and describable by mathematics, and this fits with what the Bible says: "in him all things are held together." This is a theological and philosophical inference. Science tells us what the laws are; faith tells us where the laws come from.

His Son is the radiance of his glory, the very image of his substance, and upholding all things by the word of his power, when he had by himself made purification for our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high; (Hebrews 1:3)

The universe isn't a machine you wind up and leave to run by itself; it is upheld moment by moment by God's word. The pen in your hand will fall today, and it will fall tomorrow, because there is a Lord who is "upholding all things by the word of his power."
3. Facing It Honestly: A Great Scientist Is Not a Theological Authority
At this point, if we only talked about Newton's good side, we wouldn't be honest enough.

Newton left behind a huge volume of manuscripts on theology, biblical prophecy and church history. After studying them, historians found that he privately rejected the orthodox doctrine of the Trinity, regarded it as a later corruption of the church, and believed that some Bible verses supporting the Trinity had been altered by later hands. In public, he concealed these views.
Based on his private manuscripts, there is broad consensus among Newton scholars that Newton did not accept the orthodox doctrine of the Trinity.

So how should we view Newton? We can admire Newton's reverence for God and his insight into nature, while also stating clearly that on the core doctrine of the deity of Christ, he departed from the faith of the church through the ages.

A great scientist is not a theological authority. It's like a top heart surgeon: you'd ask him to operate on you, but you wouldn't necessarily ask him to design your house. Everyone has their area of expertise, and everyone has blind spots.

Some brothers and sisters may feel a little let down hearing this: "So Newton wasn't the kind of Christian we imagined." That disappointment is normal. But I'd say this is exactly the lesson we need to learn. Our faith has never been built on "such-and-such famous person believes it too."

If someone says today, "Look, even Newton believed in God, so God must exist," that argument is actually very fragile. On the other hand, if someone says, "Look, Newton denied the Trinity, so the doctrine of the Trinity is questionable," that argument is just as fragile. Truth doesn't depend on celebrity endorsements; truth must be tested against God's Word.
The One who upholds all things is the Son

Look back at Hebrews 1:3. Who upholds all things? The very Son who "made purification for our sins." Newton saw the greatness of the laws; all the more should we know who the Lord is who gave the laws.

In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. The same was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him. Without him, nothing was made that has been made. (John 1:1–3)

"The Word was God." "All things were made through him." The laws that govern the apple, the moon and the tides were all made through this Word. This Word is Jesus Christ, who became flesh and died and rose again for us.
...Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up. (1 Corinthians 8:1)

Newton's story reminds us: however much knowledge we have, we can still go astray on the most important things. Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up. The more we understand, the more humble we must be; the smarter we are, the more we need to come back to the Bible and be taught.
Newton's greatness deserves admiration, but the example for my life is Jesus, not any celebrity. Famous people will disappoint us, because they're human too; Jesus never will.

When facing any authority's opinion, no matter how famous, how brilliant or how many awards they've won, we must go back to the Bible and test it. The Bible is my standard, not the quotations of famous people.

Knowledge puffs up. The more we understand, the more humbly we should worship. At work we often assume that the higher someone's degree or position, the more right they are; in church we might assume that the longer we've read the Bible and the more we've served, the less we need reminding. In fact, the higher we climb, the more we need to remember that we are being upheld. True wisdom doesn't make people look up at themselves; it brings them to their knees to worship the Lord who upholds all things.
This week's action: read John chapter 1, write down three statements about "who Jesus is," and share them with a friend.

Brothers and sisters, the next time something slips out of your hand, don't just bend down and pick it up. Think: this simple motion obeys the laws that govern the entire universe. And those laws are sustained by the Lord who upholds all things.
And ask yourself: do I treat brilliance as a guarantee of faith? Is the Jesus I believe in the One revealed in the Bible?

Lord Jesus, all things are held together in You. You are the Word, and You are God. Thank You for upholding all things by the word of Your power, and thank You for cleansing us from our sins. Guard our hearts, so that we are not puffed up by knowledge, but stand firm in the truth and worship You in love. In Jesus' name, Amen.

2. Newton was great in science, yet departed from orthodoxy on the core doctrine of the Trinity. What does this remind us to watch for when we hear the opinions of famous people and authorities?
3. Read John 1:1–3 and Hebrews 1:3. Who do these passages say Jesus is? What does that mean for your daily life?
Fire Sewn Into a Coat: Pascal and Boyle
You shall seek me, and find me, when you search for me with all your heart. (Jeremiah 29:13)

Brothers and sisters, friends, peace to you! Let me ask you: is there something special tucked away in your wallet or phone case? Maybe a photo of your child when they were little, maybe an old train ticket, maybe the first little note your spouse ever wrote you.
These things aren't worth any money, but you can't bear to throw them away, because they record a moment that changed your life.

Today I want to tell you a story even more special than that. The French mathematician Blaise Pascal was born in 1623 and died in 1662. After he died, a servant found a small piece of parchment sewn into the lining of his coat. It turned out that for years, every time he changed his coat, he had unpicked it and sewn it by hand into the new one.

What did a first-rate mathematician hide inside his clothes? Today we'll meet two experimenters: one met God on a "night of fire," and the other wrote his faith into his will. Two scientists, one shared devotion.
1. Pascal: The Boy Genius and the Night of Fire
Helping his father with the taxes

Pascal was a genius. As a teenager, to help his father calculate taxes, he designed a mechanical calculator. Friends, when I was a teenager, my biggest contribution to my father was probably finding the TV remote.

His scientific achievements didn't stop there. In 1648 he asked his brother-in-law Périer to measure the height of a column of mercury at the top and bottom of the Puy de Dôme mountain, and the results showed that air pressure decreases with altitude. That's why your bag of snacks puffs up when you climb a high mountain.

He also discovered "Pascal's principle": pressure in an enclosed fluid is transmitted evenly throughout. That's the principle behind today's hydraulic press. When a garage uses hydraulics to lift a whole car, Pascal's name is behind it.

In 1654 he also corresponded with another mathematician, Pierre de Fermat, laying the foundations of probability theory. Insurance today and the chance of rain in the weather forecast are both connected to this field.
In that same year, 1654, Pascal went through something that changed his whole life. The parchment sewn into his coat read:

"The year of grace 1654, Monday, 23 November... from about half past ten in the evening until about half past midnight. Fire. God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob, not of the philosophers and scholars."

Later generations called this paper the "Memorial," and that night became known as the "Night of Fire." Two hours, one word: fire. A mathematician used to speaking in precise numbers could write only this one word when he stood before God.
You shall seek me, and find me, when you search for me with all your heart. (Jeremiah 29:13)
Pascal spent his whole life seeking the truth. That night he didn't find an answer; he met a Person.

Did you notice how precisely he recorded it? The year, the month, the day, the day of the week, even the times. That's a mathematician's habit. But after all those precise numbers, he wrote just one word: fire. As if to say: I can measure the time, but what I met that night is something I cannot measure.
2. The Heart Has Reasons Reason Does Not Know
Not the God of the philosophers
Please notice the line Pascal wrote: "God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob, not of the philosophers and scholars."

Pascal was a first-rate mathematician; of course he knew how to think about God with reason. But what he met on the Night of Fire was not an abstract "First Cause," not an inference on a blackboard, but the God who made a covenant with Abraham and keeps it.
Moreover he said, "I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob." Moses hid his face; for he was afraid to look at God. (Exodus 3:6)
This is how God introduced Himself to Moses from the burning bush. Abraham, Isaac and Jacob were real people with names, with weaknesses and with stories. God is a God who walks with real people.
The flashlight and the open heart

During his life Pascal planned to write a book defending Christianity, but he died before finishing it. Others gathered his notes and published them in 1670 as the Pensées. It contains a famous line: "The heart has its reasons of which reason knows nothing."
This isn't opposing reason. What Pascal meant is that we come to know the truth not by reasoning alone, but also with the heart.

We could put it this way: reason is like a flashlight that can light up many things. But to truly know a person, a flashlight isn't enough. You can't shine a flashlight on your spouse and say, "I've finished my analysis; now I know you." Knowing a person takes trust and an open heart. Knowing God is the same.
The wager: a choice in the face of eternity

The Pensées also contains the famous "wager" argument. Many people misunderstand it as an attempt to prove God exists, but it isn't. It's a challenge: facing eternity, how will you choose? You can't stand in the doorway forever saying, "I'll wait and see." It's a philosophical and apologetic line of reasoning, meant to make people face the question seriously, not an arithmetic game.
Now let's cross the Channel to England and meet our second main character: Robert Boyle, born in 1627 and died in 1691.

In 1662 he published the inverse relationship between the pressure and volume of a gas, what we now call Boyle's law: at constant temperature, the smaller you squeeze a gas, the greater its pressure. It's like squeezing a balloon hard: the flatter you squeeze it, the harder it pushes back.

Here too I should be honest: this relationship was first proposed as a hypothesis by Henry Power and Richard Towneley, and Boyle confirmed it by experiment and published it. So who deserves the name is a matter of historical debate.

Boyle was one of the founding members of the Royal Society. He emphasized experiments, public records and results others could repeat and verify. In other words: don't just say "trust me"; write down how you did it so others can do it too. That shaped the way modern science works.
Writing his faith into his will

Boyle was also a devout Anglican. He paid for the printing of the Bible in Irish, so that more people could read God's Word in their own language. He wrote works such as The Christian Virtuoso, published in 1690.

In 1680 he was elected President of the Royal Society, an extremely high honor in the scientific world of the time. But he declined it, because he had scruples of conscience about taking the required oaths. Laying down such a lofty position over a matter of conscience took great courage.

Today we often do the opposite: for the sake of a position, we're willing to put our conscience in a drawer for a while. "Everyone does it." "It's just a formality." "Just this once." Boyle reminds us that a tender conscience is more precious than an impressive title. People will forget the title, but your conscience goes with you to meet the Lord.

Most remarkable of all, in his will he established a lecture series devoted to defending the Christian faith: the "Boyle Lectures." Richard Bentley gave the first ones in 1692. And in 2004 the lectures were revived in London.
Just think about it: more than three hundred years after a man died, the seeds he sowed in his will are still sprouting.
Yahweh, how many are your works! In wisdom have you made them all. The earth is full of your riches. (Psalm 104:24)
Pascal measured the pressure of the air; Boyle measured the volume of gases. Both of them studied the invisible air. Yet in that invisible air, both of them saw the wisdom of God.
Science lets us see God's works; but to know God Himself, we need Him to reveal Himself, and we need our hearts to be open to Him.
Use the heart and rely on the Holy Spirit

Pascal said the heart has reasons that reason doesn't know. Let's not only use our heads and rely on ourselves, but use our hearts and rely on the Holy Spirit. Reading the Bible isn't just gathering information, and prayer isn't just going through a list; it's opening our hearts to meet God.
Life first, then relationships, then ministry

Pascal's science and apologetics, and Boyle's research and lectures, all flowed out of their life relationship with God. First came the Night of Fire, then the Pensées; first a devoted life, then a ministry that influenced later generations. The depth of our ministry will never exceed the depth of our life.

Boyle invested his resources in translating the Bible and endowing the lectures, so that the faith would be passed on generation after generation. We may not have his wealth, but every one of us can invest in the faith of the next generation: read the Bible with a child, study Scripture with a new friend, pray for a young person.

This week's action: write down one experience of truly meeting God, and keep it somewhere you always carry, on your phone or in your wallet. This week, find a chance to share it with someone. That will be your own "Memorial."
Brothers and sisters, Pascal sewed the night he met God into his coat and carried it with him until he died. So what is the sign of your encounter with God?

Please reflect: is the God I know a concept from a book, or a God I have personally met and walk with every day? If you haven't had that experience yet, today's verse is a promise for you: "You shall seek me, and find me, when you search for me with all your heart."

God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, we don't just want to know about You; we want to know You. Thank You that You are a covenant-keeping, faithful God who meets people personally. Kindle our hearts with Your fire, help us seek You with all our hearts, and make our lives a bridge for others to come to know You. In Jesus' name, Amen.
1. Pascal sewed his "Memorial" into his coat and carried it everywhere. Has there been a moment in your life when you truly met God? Would you share it with the group?
2. "Reason is like a flashlight, but knowing a person also takes trust and an open heart." What roles do you think reason and faith each play in your life of faith?
3. Boyle used his will to endow lectures that passed the faith on to later generations. What concrete ways can you invest in the faith of the next generation?
The Painter and the Composer: Faraday and Maxwell Unlock the Secret of Light
Yahweh's works are great, pondered by all those who delight in them. (Psalm 111:2)

Brothers and sisters, friends, peace to you! Take a look at your hands and your pockets. How many of you brought a phone today? Right, almost everyone. Now think about the lights and fridge in your home, and the power station far away that runs day and night.

Behind all of these lies the same discovery: a changing magnetic field can produce an electric current. In 1831, the Englishman Michael Faraday discovered electromagnetic induction. In other words, if you can scroll on your phone and switch on a light today, you have this gentleman to thank.
Interestingly, in that same year, 1831, a baby was born in Scotland named James Clerk Maxwell. Some thirty years later, that child would use a few equations to unite electricity, magnetism and light.

Today's subtitle is: a bookbinder's apprentice who never went to university, and a mathematical genius; together they unlocked the secret of light. It's a story about a relay race, about complementing one another, and about humility.
1. The Bookbinder's Apprentice Who Painted Lines of Force
Faraday was born in 1791 and died in 1867. He was a blacksmith's son, served as a bookbinder's apprentice, and had almost no formal education.

Imagine a teenage boy in a bindery, sewing books and gluing spines for other people, with other people's learning passing through his hands every day. By attending Sir Humphry Davy's lectures and studying hard on his own, he went on to become the master experimenter of the Royal Institution in Britain.
His story is a huge encouragement to anyone who thinks, "I don't have much education; God probably can't use me."

Brothers and sisters, God doesn't look at your diploma. He looks for a heart that is willing to learn and willing to be faithful. The bookbinder's apprentice spent his days stitching other people's books, but God wanted to write a book of his own in his life. Your background and your education cannot limit what God wants to do through you.

What is the electromagnetic induction Faraday discovered? It's simple: move a magnet inside a coil of wire, and the coil produces an electric current. That's the principle behind generators and transformers.
The giant machines in a power station, when you get down to it, just keep a magnetic field and coils "dancing" together, and as they dance, out comes electricity.

Faraday also had a brilliant piece of imagination. He pictured the space around a magnet filled with invisible "lines of force," like invisible rubber bands stretching from one end of the magnet to the other.

That idea later grew into the very important concept of the "field" in physics. A man who had never studied advanced mathematics used his eyes and his imagination to see an invisible structure in space.
2. The Composer Who Set the Picture to Music
Maxwell was born in 1831 and died in 1879. He was the exact opposite of Faraday: a mathematical genius.

He wrote Faraday's pictures in the language of mathematics and in 1865 published his theory of the electromagnetic field. He calculated that the speed of electromagnetic waves equals the speed of light. From this he drew an astonishing conclusion: light is an electromagnetic wave.
Friends, from then on electricity, magnetism and light were no longer three unrelated things, but members of the same family.

We could put it this way: Faraday was like a painter, drawing the picture of the lines of force with his eyes and hands; Maxwell was like a composer, setting that picture to a symphony of mathematics. One relied on experiment, the other on mathematics, and only together did they see the whole picture.

After Maxwell's death, his theory was confirmed when Heinrich Hertz, in the late 1880s, produced and detected electromagnetic waves experimentally. Today's radio, radar and Wi-Fi are all built on that foundation.
So the next time your Wi-Fi at home is slow, please don't blame Maxwell. He did his best.

Did you notice that this was a relay race across generations? Faraday drew the picture, Maxwell composed the music, and Hertz actually performed it. None of the three could have done it alone. God's kingdom is like that too: one plants, one waters, one reaps; every leg of the race matters, and none is unnecessary.
Elegant equations point to a faithful Creator

That electricity, magnetism and light in nature can be united by a few elegant equations is itself astonishing. Light travels about 300,000 kilometers every second, yet it obediently follows a few simple equations.
This leads us to reasonably infer that behind it all is a faithful and wise Creator. This is a philosophical inference, not an experimental conclusion, but it is a beautiful pointer.
3. The Verse Carved Over the Laboratory Door
These two scientists didn't just complement each other in science; they were equally devout in faith.

Faraday belonged to a very small denomination called the Sandemanians. He made a public profession of faith in 1821, later served twice as an elder, and often visited poor and sick members of the church.

Think about it: a world-class scientist leaves his laboratory and goes to visit the sick. Those poor and sick church members may not have understood the first thing about electromagnetic induction, but they knew that Elder Faraday would come to see them. In God's eyes, those visits were just as precious as his discoveries in the lab. He turned down a knighthood, and twice turned down the presidency of the Royal Society. He preferred to remain plain "Mr. Faraday."

In an 1854 lecture, he said, in substance (our paraphrase), that God's works in nature can never contradict the higher things that belong to our future life. He was settled in his heart: studying nature and hoping for eternal life do not conflict at all.
A psalm carved over the door

In 1871 Maxwell became the first Cavendish Professor of Experimental Physics at the University of Cambridge and oversaw the building of the Cavendish Laboratory. Over the laboratory's great door, Psalm 111:2 was carved in Latin.

It is generally believed that Maxwell chose this verse. Here I need to be honest: most sources say so, but direct documentary evidence from the time is scarce, so we say "it is generally believed." When the new laboratory was completed in 1973, the same verse was also carved in English at the entrance.
Yahweh's works are great, pondered by all those who delight in them. (Psalm 111:2)

Friends, at one of the world's top physics laboratories, every scientist coming and going looks up and sees these words: the works of the Lord are great, pondered by all who delight in them. This isn't shutting faith out of the laboratory; it's placing faith right at the laboratory's door.

Maxwell was wholeheartedly involved in church life all his life. In a letter to his wife he wrote, in words to this effect (our paraphrase): the more we enter together into the work of Christ, the more room He has to do His work in us.
Maxwell discovered that light is an electromagnetic wave, but the Bible tells us the source of light.
God said, "Let there be light," and there was light. (Genesis 1:3)
This is the message which we have heard from him and announce to you, that God is light, and in him is no darkness at all. (1 John 1:5)
Physical light lets us see the world; Jesus, the true Light, lets us see the path of life.

Think about it: even if a room is full of the finest furniture, without the light on you'll just keep bumping into table legs. Life is the same: filled with learning, wealth and achievement, yet without the true Light we still can't see which way to go. Scientists can tell us what light is, but only Jesus can tell us where to walk in the light.
Again, therefore, Jesus spoke to them, saying, "I am the light of the world. He who follows me will not walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life." (John 8:12)
Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom can be no variation, nor turning shadow. (James 1:17)
Faraday turned down a knighthood and chose to be plain "Mr. Faraday." Those who let Jesus reign don't need to chase human glory. When Jesus reigns in my heart, I don't need a title to prove my worth.

Faraday and Maxwell, one with experiments, one with mathematics, completed each other. We also need spiritual companions (the "235" pattern of walking together in faith) who complement us. What you're good at may be exactly what someone else lacks; what someone else is good at may be exactly what you need. Don't try to be a one-man band; God wants us to form a choir.

Carving a psalm over the laboratory door was a declaration of God's sovereignty in the workplace. Building God's kingdom system happens not only in church, but in your company, your school and your home.

This week's action: put a Bible verse on your desk, at your workplace or as your phone wallpaper, for example Psalm 111:2, and read it every day before you start work. Let your workplace have a door with a verse carved over it too.

Brothers and sisters, when you go home today, turn on a light and watch it fill the room. Think about how that light travels about 300,000 kilometers every second, yet obeys a few simple equations. And think about how the God who said "Let there be light" also wants to shine into the darkness of your heart.
Please reflect: do I delight in God's works? Am I willing to take time to "ponder" His work in my life?

Father of lights, thank You for saying "Let there be light," and for sending Jesus to be the light of the world. Thank You for using both a humble bookbinder's apprentice and a mathematical genius to show us the greatness of Your works. Shine into the darkness of our hearts, help us follow You, and make us a light to others. In Jesus' name, Amen.

2. Faraday relied on experiment and Maxwell on mathematics, and they completed each other. In your life or ministry, who is a spiritual companion who complements you?

Peas in the Monastery Garden: Mendel and Unseen Faithfulness
I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase. (1 Corinthians 3:6)

Brothers and sisters, friends, peace to you! Have you ever heard a conversation like this at home? Relatives come to see the new baby, and the first thing someone says is, "Oh, the eyes are just like Dad's!" Someone else immediately says, "No, no, the mouth is Mom's!" Then Grandma walks out of the kitchen and says, "You're all wrong. That temper? That's his grandpa."
Everyone laughs. But behind it lies a very old question: why do children take after Dad in some ways and Mom in others, and why do some traits "skip a generation" before showing up again?

Before the nineteenth century, people generally assumed that parents' traits blended together like paint. A tall father and a short mother make a medium child; a red father and a white mother make a pink child. But if that were really true, where did that "grandpa's temper" jump out from?
The answer was found in an unexpected place: the small vegetable garden of a monastery. Today's subtitle is: in a monastery's little garden, a friar growing peas discovered the laws of heredity.
In the Abbey of St Thomas in Brno, in today's Czech Republic, lived an Augustinian friar named Gregor Mendel, born in 1822 and died in 1884. He was a Catholic priest, and a very patient researcher.

He spent years growing and counting tens of thousands of peas. Friends, tens of thousands! Most of us find shelling one bowl of peas tedious, yet he counted them one by one and recorded them plant by plant.

Can you picture it? A vegetable garden in summer, the sun blazing, a man in a friar's habit crouching among the pea vines with a little notebook, writing down plant after plant: what color flowers this one has, whether that pea is round or wrinkled. People passing by probably thought, "What on earth is that friar doing?" What he was doing looked completely unremarkable at the time.

Why did Mendel choose peas? Because peas are easy to grow, their pollination can be controlled, and they have very clear contrasting traits, such as seeds that are round or wrinkled, yellow or green. Nothing ambiguous, nothing "a bit round and a bit wrinkled."
He tracked seven pairs of traits altogether: flower color, seed shape, seed color, pod shape, pod color, flower position and plant height.
Now comes the most exciting part. He crossed pure-bred round peas with wrinkled peas, and the first generation all came out round. The wrinkled trait seemed to have vanished.

But when he let the first generation pollinate themselves, the wrinkled peas came back in the second generation! And the ratio of round to wrinkled was about three to one. In other words, the recessive wrinkled trait reappeared in the second generation, making up about a quarter.
From this Mendel reasoned that heredity is determined by paired "factors" that do not blend. Today we call those factors genes.
A deck of cards, not paint

Let's think of it with a picture. Heredity isn't like mixing red and white paint into pink, which you can never undo; heredity is more like a deck of cards. Every card stays as it is; each generation the deck is simply reshuffled and dealt again.

A card that was face down, that is, a recessive trait, may not be turned up this round, but it can be turned up the next. So when Grandma says the child's temper is like Grandpa's, maybe she isn't entirely joking; that card may just have been face down for a round.

When you go home, you could do a little survey: do you have some trait that neither of your parents has, but that's exactly like your grandpa or grandma? You might discover that you're holding a few cards that were face down for a round.

Friends, a stable, predictable law lets life pass from generation to generation. This leads us to reasonably infer that behind it is an orderly and faithful Creator. This is a philosophical inference, not an experimental conclusion, but it is a beautiful pointer.
In February and March of 1865, Mendel read his paper to the Natural Science Society in Brno, and in 1866 it was published in volume 4 of the Society's proceedings.

Do you think what came next was thunderous applause and worldwide fame? No. Hardly anyone at the time saw its importance. Once published, the paper just lay there quietly, like a seed buried in the ground.
He used statistics and mathematics to tackle biological questions, which was very cutting-edge at the time. Maybe it was too cutting-edge, and people just couldn't understand it yet.

In 1868 Mendel was elected abbot of the monastery. From then on his administrative workload was very heavy, and his research gradually dwindled. Anyone who has served as a volunteer leader or small-group leader knows: once you start managing things, you often no longer have time for what you love to do most.

That's very true to life, and worth reflecting on. Life doesn't always follow our interests. Sometimes God puts us in a position that isn't our favorite, but it's where we are needed at that time. Being faithful there is a kind of planting too.
In 1884 Mendel died. In his lifetime, he never saw his discovery recognized.
It wasn't until 1900 that his paper was rediscovered by several scientists, more than thirty years after he published it. Mendel came to be honored as the "father of genetics."
Think about it: a man labored quietly all his life and went unseen right up to his death. But on God's timetable his work was not wasted; the seed was simply still in the ground.

Our lives have many seeds like that. A mother reads the Bible and prays with her child every night, and the child never seems to be listening; a Sunday school teacher teaches for many years, and the students leave when they grow up; a brother quietly holds on to honesty at his company, and nobody praises him. Brothers and sisters, none of this is wasted. It may take many years, or it may not be until the day you see the Lord face to face, that you find out what that seed grew into.
So then neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase. (1 Corinthians 3:7)

Paul says that neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but God who gives the increase. Mendel did the planting and the counting of peas; it was God who made those discoveries grow and bear fruit thirty-some years later.
3. Looking Honestly, and Seeing God's Wisdom in Small Things

In talking about Mendel, we should also honestly mention a controversy. In 1936 the statistician Ronald Fisher pointed out that Mendel's data were "too good to be true," and suspected that someone had adjusted them.

The debate went on for decades. In 2008 a book co-authored by several scholars pulled together the various analyses; most concluded there is no evidence that Mendel deliberately falsified anything, but there are still different explanations for why the data came so close to what was expected.
We mention this not to take points away from him, but to learn an attitude: when we tell a hero's story, we tell the question marks too. Truth isn't afraid of being examined.

This is actually a freedom our faith gives us. We don't need to portray God's people as flawless, because the One we trust was never a perfect human being, but a perfect God. People leave question marks behind; God is faithful forever.

There's one more thing we should be honest about. Part of the reason Mendel entered the monastery was so that he could get an education for free and be spared financial worries. There is little historical evidence about how his faith related to his motives for research, and we shouldn't overdramatize it.

So today we won't package Mendel as a spiritual giant who "grew peas for the glory of God." We simply see that in a monastery garden, through a friar faithfully counting peas, God revealed the laws of life.
Great laws revealed in small things
Mendel's discovery came from the most ordinary of places: a monastery garden, one pea after another. God often reveals His great wisdom in small things.

He set another parable before them, saying, "The Kingdom of Heaven is like a grain of mustard seed which a man took, and sowed in his field, which indeed is smaller than all seeds. But when it is grown, it is greater than the herbs, and becomes a tree, so that the birds of the air come and lodge in its branches." (Matthew 13:31–32)

The Lord Jesus said the kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed, the smallest of all seeds, which grows into a tree. A single pea grew into a whole field of science; a mustard seed grew into a great tree where birds nest. Brothers and sisters, don't despise the small thing in your hands.
From the temporary to the eternal

Mendel was not recognized in his lifetime, but faithful work in God's hands never comes to nothing. We often look at our efforts through "temporary" eyes: did anyone like it? did anyone notice? But from the perspective of eternity, God remembers every pea you have counted.

Mendel counted peas day after day. Change in our lives also takes repeated practice; it isn't done all at once. Reading the Bible, praying, learning to forgive: do it today, and do it again tomorrow. Those days that seem repetitive and boring are exactly the days God is shaping you.

It's like learning to ride a bicycle: nobody learns just by watching a video once. You fall, you get up, and you ride again; the tenth time is a little steadier than the first, and one day you can let go and ride on. The spiritual life is like that; every repetition paves a road in your heart.

When the results come, give the credit to God who gives the increase, not to yourself. Neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything. This doesn't mean our effort is unimportant; it means that it is God who makes everything grow.

We can ask ourselves a question: the last time something worked out, what was the first thing I said? "Good thing I worked so hard," or "Thank You, Lord"? Both can be said, but which one comes out first often reveals where our hearts place the glory.

This week's action: choose one small thing you're doing that no one sees, perhaps cleaning, perhaps interceding for someone, perhaps caring for family. Do it faithfully every day this week, and offer it to God in prayer.
Brothers and sisters, when you go home today, look in the mirror. See the ways you resemble your parents, and see the ways you are uniquely you. Every one of you is God's carefully crafted work.
Please reflect: have I become discouraged because my efforts go unseen? Am I willing to hand the results over to the God who gives the increase?

God who makes all things grow, thank You for showing Your wisdom in ordinary things, and for hiding the laws of life in pea after pea. Help us to be faithful where no one sees, not to lose heart in repetitive days, and to leave the results in Your hands. May all the fruit bring glory to You. In Jesus' name, Amen.
