The Telescope and the Letter: A Dialogue Between Science and Faith

For the invisible things of him since the creation of the world are clearly seen, being perceived through the things that are made, even his everlasting power and divinity, that they may be without excuse. (Romans 1:20)
Brothers and sisters, friends, peace to you! Let me start with a quiz: who was one of the pioneers of the idea that "the universe had a beginning"?
Many people would guess it was some bespectacled physicist who didn't go to church much. The answer may surprise you: it was a Catholic priest.

His name was Georges Lemaître, a Belgian, born in 1894 and died in 1966. In 1927 he proposed that the universe is expanding; in 1931, in the journal Nature, he proposed that the universe began from a "primeval atom." This was the forerunner of the Big Bang theory.
In 1933, in an interview with The New York Times, he said: "There were two ways of arriving at the truth. I decided to follow them both."

Today is the last unit of the History of Science Hall. We've walked with Kepler, Galileo, Newton, Pascal, Boyle, Faraday, Maxwell and Mendel, and today we'll close with Lemaître's words: science and faith are not eternal enemies, but friends who can have an honest conversation.
1. Where Did the Idea of "Endless War" Come From?
Many people carry an impression that science and religion have always been at war. On one side the laboratory, on the other the church, two armies facing off, irreconcilable.

Where did that impression come from? In large part from two books of the late nineteenth century: John William Draper's History of the Conflict between Religion and Science, published in 1874, and Andrew Dickson White's A History of the Warfare of Science with Theology in Christendom, published in 1896.
You can tell just from the titles: one is a "history of conflict," the other a "history of warfare." With titles like that, the contents were hardly going to read like a "history of friendship."

Most historians of science today believe these two books had an obvious agenda and reduced a complex history to a war. In reality, the relationship between science and faith has included conflict, but also cooperation, independence and dialogue, varying by era and by person.

Most historians of science regard the conflict thesis, that "science and religion have always been at war," as mainly a nineteenth-century construction that oversimplifies history. What we've seen in this hall is exactly that kind of complex and rich history: the pain of the Galileo affair, and also the beauty of Kepler, Faraday and Maxwell joining their research with worship.
Do scientists not believe in God?
Another common impression is that scientists don't believe in God. What are the facts?

In 2009, the Pew Research Center surveyed scientists who were members of the American Association for the Advancement of Science: about 33% believed in God, 18% believed in a universal spirit or higher power, and 41% believed in neither. Taken together, about 51% believed in God or some higher power, a lower proportion than the general American public.

The research of sociologist Elaine Howard Ecklund has also found that the religious landscape among scientists is more diverse than commonly assumed. So the claim that "if you're a scientist you can't believe in God" doesn't match reality.
Two tools for knowing the same friend
So what is the relationship between science and faith? Let's think about it with a picture.
Science and faith are like a telescope and a letter. The telescope lets you see clearly how tall a distant mountain is; the letter lets you understand that the one who wrote it loves you.

If you tried to read the letter with the telescope, you'd probably just see a magnified blob of ink; if you tried to measure the mountain with the letter, however moving it was, it couldn't tell you how many meters high the mountain is. Use the wrong tool, and you'll get both wrong. But the two together can help you know the same friend: He made this mountain, and He wrote this letter.

Science describes how creation works, but it cannot, on its own, answer "why does anything exist at all?" The order of creation points to a Creator; this is a philosophical inference. Science is the telescope; the Bible is the letter.
Lemaître himself was very careful about this. He didn't let scientific theory and theology get mixed up.

In 1951, Pope Pius XII gave an address that seemed to equate the beginning of the universe directly with the creation described in the Bible. Guess how Lemaître reacted? Was he delighted? No, he was uneasy.

Why? Because scientific theories can be revised, and faith shouldn't be tied to any one scientific model. It's like building a house's foundation on a boat: when the boat moves, the house shakes with it. Our faith should be built on God's unchanging Word, not on a theory that may be revised.

This is very helpful for many debates today. For example, Christians hold different views on the age of the earth and on the mechanisms of biological change. We should be "united on the core and generous on the periphery": standing firm on the core truths that God created all things and that Christ redeems us, and bearing with one another on the details of scientific models.
Let me introduce a contemporary example: the American geneticist Francis Collins. He led the Human Genome Project and served as director of the U.S. National Institutes of Health.
At the age of 27 he read C. S. Lewis's Mere Christianity and came to faith. In 2006 he published The Language of God, and in 2007 he founded BioLogos, devoted to dialogue between science and faith.
You see, a scientist who read the code of the human genome also read and understood God's love. He held both the telescope and the letter in his hands.

For the invisible things of him since the creation of the world are clearly seen, being perceived through the things that are made, even his everlasting power and divinity, that they may be without excuse. (Romans 1:20)

God's everlasting power and divinity can be perceived through the things He has made. That is the heart of all of Creation Speaks: the created world is a window through which we see the invisible God.
Whatever is true comes from Him
Having walked through this hall, we see one thing: God is the source of all truth. Whether in the laboratory or in the Bible, whatever is true comes from Him.
For with you is the spring of life. In your light we will see light. (Psalm 36:9)
So Christians don't need to be afraid of truth. If a discovery is true, it is God's truth; if a claim is false, time and testing will expose it. We can learn with confidence and with open minds.
The fear of God is where knowledge begins
Still, science lets us see God's works but cannot replace God's Word. The fear of God is the true starting point of all knowledge.
The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of knowledge; but the foolish despise wisdom and instruction. (Proverbs 1:7)

Notice that it says "beginning." It isn't that after we've mastered all learning we add a little reverence at the end as decoration; from the very start, the fear of the Lord is the foundation. With that foundation, knowledge won't puff us up.
Dim now, face to face then
Finally, we must humbly admit that whether in science or theology, what we know now is limited.
For now we see in a mirror, dimly, but then face to face. Now I know in part, but then I will know fully, even as I was also fully known. (1 Corinthians 13:12)

Today we're like people solving riddles: scientists are guessing, theologians are guessing; sometimes we guess right, and sometimes we need correcting. But one day we will see the Lord face to face. On that day every riddle will have its answer. Until then, we keep exploring and keep talking, with humility.

Scientific discoveries can enrich our understanding of the world, but the direction of our lives is set by the Bible. The telescope tells me how tall the mountain is, but only the letter tells me which way to go.

When talking with people who see things differently, care about the person first, then discuss the ideas; don't mock and don't belittle. The friend across from you with questions about faith is not an opponent to defeat, but someone God loves who is searching. Winning a debate but losing a friend is not victory.
Let Jesus receive all the glory

Whether scientists or ordinary people, all discoveries belong to the Lord who made all things. Kepler's orbits, Newton's laws, Faraday and Maxwell's light, Mendel's peas: in the end they all give glory to the same Lord.

This week's action: find a friend who has questions about faith, buy them a cup of coffee, ask them one sincere question, and then listen patiently without rushing to argue. Sometimes the most powerful witness isn't a brilliant argument, but a pair of ears willing to listen.

Brothers and sisters, congratulations: together we've finished the History of Science Hall! From the birth of modern science, to Kepler's orbits, Newton's laws, Faraday and Maxwell's light, Mendel's peas, and on to today's dialogue, we have seen a faithful, wise and righteous God who keeps inviting people to explore His works.

Think back over the people in this hall: Kepler, Galileo, Newton, Pascal, Boyle, Faraday, Maxwell, Mendel, Lemaître. Each had strengths and each had weaknesses, but all of them searched for truth within creation.
Please reflect: have I ever avoided questions because I was afraid of science, or looked down on faith because I worshiped science?

Lord of all truth, thank You for letting all created things declare Your glory, and thank You for speaking to us through Your Word. Help us to fear You and love the truth, not to be afraid of questions, nor to worship knowledge. In the dialogue between science and faith, help us bear witness to You with gentleness and humility. In Jesus' name, Amen.
